unit.unitOverview: The Earth is one of eight planets going round one star, with a moon of its own going round it. This unit puts those motions in order, explains why the Moon appears to change shape when it never does, and shows how both facts come from the same cause: things in space moving in paths set by gravity.

objectives.text: Describe the relative position and movement of the planets, the Moon and the Sun in the Solar System.
Observe and describe the changes in the appearance of the Moon over its monthly cycle.

sourceDocuments: Cambridge Primary Science Teacher's Resource 6, topics on the Solar System and the Moon

outcomes: Name the eight planets in order from the Sun.
Describe the relative positions of the Sun, the planets and the Moon.
Explain what orbits what, and what holds each orbit in place.
Describe the Moon's phases over a month.
Explain why the Moon appears to change shape when it does not.
Tell the difference between a star, a planet and a moon.

concepts.title: The Solar System, in Order
concepts.explanation:
At the centre of the Solar System is the SUN, and the first thing to be clear about is what it is: a STAR, one of countless billions, and the only object in the Solar System that makes its own light. Everything else we see out there is shining with light borrowed from it.

Eight PLANETS orbit the Sun. In order outwards: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune. The first four are small and rocky; the outer four are enormous and made mostly of gas and ice. Between Mars and Jupiter is a belt of rocky rubble called asteroids.

The distances are the part worth dwelling on, because diagrams cannot show them honestly. If the Sun were the size of a football, the Earth would be a grain of sand about 25 metres away, and Neptune would be another grain three quarters of a kilometre off. Almost all of the Solar System is empty space.

A MOON is an object that orbits a planet rather than the Sun. The Earth has one; Jupiter has more than ninety. So there is a clear ladder: moons orbit planets, planets orbit the Sun, and the Sun is a star.

What holds it all together is GRAVITY. The Sun is so massive that its gravity reaches out past Neptune and keeps every planet curving round it instead of flying off in a straight line. The Earth's own gravity does the same job for the Moon, on a much smaller scale.

The farther out a planet is, the longer its year, because it has further to travel and moves more slowly. Mercury goes round in 88 days; Earth takes 365; Neptune takes about 165 Earth years.
concepts.example: Look at the night sky and you can see two quite different kinds of point. The stars twinkle and stay in fixed patterns night after night. The planets - Venus and Jupiter are the brightest - shine steadily and slowly change position against the stars from week to week, which is how the word 'planet', meaning wanderer, was earned.

concepts.title: What Goes Round What
concepts.explanation:
Three motions are happening at once, and confusing them is the commonest difficulty in this whole subject. Take them one at a time.

The Earth SPINS on its own axis, once in 24 hours. That gives day and night: the side facing the Sun is lit and the side facing away is dark, and every place passes through both as it turns. Nothing about the Sun moving is involved - the Sun appears to cross the sky because we are the ones rotating.

The Earth ORBITS the Sun, once in about 365 days. That is a year, and it is a much slower motion, going on all the time underneath the daily spin.

The MOON orbits the Earth, once in about 27 days, while being carried round the Sun along with us.

So the Moon goes round the Earth, the Earth goes round the Sun, and the Earth spins all the while. Three motions, three different periods, all at once.

The tell for whether you have it straight is this question: does the Sun go round the Earth? It does not, and it never has - but it certainly looks as if it does, and for most of human history that was the sensible conclusion from the available evidence. What settled it was careful records of where the planets appear night after night, which only make sense if the Earth is one of the things going round.

One more point worth fixing. The Moon keeps the same face towards us always, because it turns once on its own axis in exactly the time it takes to go round us. There is no permanently dark side - the far side gets just as much sunlight; we simply never see it.
concepts.example: Stand a lamp on a table for the Sun, hold a ball for the Earth and walk slowly round the lamp while spinning the ball. Every spin is a day. One lap is a year. Now have someone circle a smaller ball round yours as you walk - that is the Moon, doing its own lap while being carried round the lamp with you.

concepts.title: Why the Moon Seems to Change Shape
concepts.explanation:
Watch the Moon for a month and it appears to change shape completely: a thin crescent, then half, then a full bright circle, then shrinking back and vanishing. It does none of this. The Moon is a ball, always, and it is always exactly half lit by the Sun - the same as the Earth is. What changes is how much of that lit half we can see from here.

The Moon has no light of its own. It shines with reflected sunlight, which is why the lit part always faces the Sun.

As the Moon goes round us, our viewing angle changes. When it is roughly between us and the Sun, its lit half faces away and we see almost nothing - a NEW MOON. A week later we are looking at it side-on and see exactly half of the lit half, which appears as a half circle - the FIRST QUARTER. A week after that the Moon is on the far side from the Sun, its whole lit half faces us, and we see a FULL MOON. Another week gives the LAST QUARTER, and then it thins back to new.

The whole cycle takes about 29 and a half days, which is where a month comes from.

The usual mistake is to think the phases are the Earth's shadow falling on the Moon. They are not - that is an eclipse, which is a rare event, and phases happen every month without fail. The phases are simply geometry: a half-lit ball, seen from changing angles.

Waxing means the lit part is growing; waning means it is shrinking.
concepts.example: Hold a ball at arm's length in a dark room with a single lamp to one side. Turn slowly on the spot, keeping the ball in front of you, and watch it: a crescent, then half, then fully lit, then back. The ball never changed and the lamp never moved. Only your angle did.

concepts.title: Star, Planet, Moon
concepts.explanation:
Three words that get used loosely, and the differences are precise and worth having.

A STAR makes its own light, by reactions in its core, and is enormous. The Sun is a star, and an ordinary one - it looks special only because it is close. Every other star you can see is far enough away to be a point of light however much you magnify it.

A PLANET makes no light of its own. It is a large object orbiting a star, shining only by reflecting that star's light, and it is round because its own gravity pulled it into a ball. There are eight in our Solar System.

A MOON is a natural object orbiting a PLANET. It also makes no light of its own. Our Moon is one; Jupiter has more than ninety, some of them larger than Mercury.

So the difference between a planet and a moon is not size but what it goes round. And the difference between a star and the other two is whether it makes its own light.

There is one more word worth adding. A SATELLITE is anything that orbits something larger, so our Moon is a natural satellite of the Earth - and the spacecraft we launch are artificial ones, doing the same job by design: relaying telephone calls, photographing weather systems, and showing farmers where rain has fallen.

A quick test: if it makes its own light it is a star; if it does not and goes round a star it is a planet; if it does not and goes round a planet it is a moon.
concepts.example: On a clear night, the brightest object after the Moon is often Venus - and it is a planet, reflecting sunlight, not a star. It gives itself away by not twinkling, and by having moved against the star patterns when you look again a fortnight later.

explorations.title: Making the Phases with a Ball
explorations.context: To show that the Moon's phases come from the viewing angle and not from any change in the Moon.
explorations.prompt: In a darkened room, put one lamp on a table. Hold a pale ball at arm's length and turn slowly on the spot, keeping the ball in front of you. Draw what the ball looks like at four points a quarter turn apart.
explorations.answer: The ball appears as a crescent, then half lit, then fully lit, then half the other way - the Moon's phases exactly. The ball never changed shape and the lamp never moved.
explorations.hint: Keep the ball at the same height and the same distance the whole way round, or you will be changing two things at once.
explorations.explanation: Why the Moon Seems to Change Shape: the Moon is always a half-lit ball, and the phases are how much of the lit half happens to face us.

explorations.title: A Month of Moon Watching
explorations.context: To record the Moon's phases over time and find the length of the cycle from your own data.
explorations.prompt: Every clear evening for four weeks, sketch the Moon's shape and write the date. Then work out how many days passed between one full moon and the next.
explorations.answer: About 29 and a half days from full moon to full moon. The shape changes in a repeating, predictable cycle - and the record proves it in a way that remembering cannot.
explorations.hint: Sketch it even on the nights it looks the same as yesterday - the gaps in a record are what make the count wrong.
explorations.explanation: Why the Moon Seems to Change Shape: the cycle takes about 29 and a half days, which is where the month came from.

explorations.title: The Solar System to Scale
explorations.context: To find out how misleading every picture of the Solar System is about distance.
explorations.prompt: Take a football as the Sun. A grain of sand 25 m away is the Earth. Work out where Neptune would be, then pace it out if you have the room.
explorations.answer: Neptune would be about 750 m away - three quarters of a kilometre from the football. Almost all of the Solar System is empty space, which no diagram that fits on a page can show.
explorations.hint: Neptune is about thirty times as far from the Sun as the Earth is, so multiply your 25 m by thirty.
explorations.explanation: The Solar System, in Order: the planets orbit at distances so large that any diagram showing them all on one page must shrink the gaps enormously.

methods.title: Is It a Star, a Planet or a Moon?
methods.example: To classify an object in the sky from what it does rather than how bright it looks.
steps: Ask whether it makes its own light. If it does, it is a star.
If it does not, ask what it orbits.
Orbiting a star makes it a planet; orbiting a planet makes it a moon.
Check with two observations: a star twinkles and holds its place in a pattern; a planet shines steadily and shifts against the stars over weeks.
Write down which observation decided it.

methods.title: Explaining a Phase
methods.example: To say why the Moon looks the way it does tonight.
steps: Draw the Sun, the Earth and the Moon in a line or at a right angle as tonight requires.
Shade the half of the Moon that faces away from the Sun - that half is always dark.
Mark where you are on the Earth and look along your line of sight to the Moon.
Work out how much of the LIT half you can see from there.
Name the phase, and say whether it is waxing or waning.

methods.title: Keeping Three Motions Apart
methods.example: To describe what causes day, a year and a month without confusing them.
steps: Name the motion: is it a spin on an axis, or an orbit round something?
Say what is moving and what it is moving around.
Give its period - 24 hours, 27 days, 365 days.
Say what we observe because of it - day and night, the Moon's phases, the seasons.
Check you have not made the Sun move: it does not go round us, however it looks.

workedExamples.title: Naming the planets in order
workedExamples.prompt: List the eight planets from the Sun outwards, and say which are rocky.
workedExamples.solution: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune. The first four - Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars - are the small rocky ones. The outer four are giants made mostly of gas and ice, with a belt of asteroids between Mars and Jupiter.

workedExamples.title: Why day and night are not caused by the Sun moving
workedExamples.prompt: The Sun appears to cross the sky each day. Explain what is actually happening.
workedExamples.solution: The Earth is spinning on its axis, once in 24 hours. The side facing the Sun is in daylight and the side facing away is in darkness, and every place passes through both as the Earth turns. The Sun is not moving across the sky; we are rotating past it, which produces exactly the same appearance.

workedExamples.title: Why a full moon happens
workedExamples.prompt: Explain the positions of the Sun, Earth and Moon at full moon.
workedExamples.solution: At full moon the Earth is roughly between the Sun and the Moon. The Sun lights the half of the Moon facing it, and because that is also the half facing us, we see the whole lit circle. Two weeks later the Moon is on the other side, its lit half faces away from us, and we see almost nothing - a new moon.

workedExamples.title: Phases are not eclipses
workedExamples.prompt: A friend says the phases happen because the Earth's shadow falls on the Moon. Explain why that cannot be right.
workedExamples.solution: If the phases were the Earth's shadow they would happen only when the three bodies lined up exactly, which is rare - that IS an eclipse, and eclipses happen a few times a year. Phases happen every single month, without fail, and pass through the whole cycle. They are caused by our changing view of a permanently half-lit ball, not by any shadow.

activities.title: Three motions with three people
activities.materials: A lamp or torch, a large ball, a small ball, and a dark room.
steps: Stand the lamp in the middle as the Sun. One person holds the large ball as the Earth and spins it slowly while walking round the lamp.
A second person carries the small ball round the Earth as it walks.
Count one spin as a day, one lap of the lamp as a year, one lap of the Earth as a month.
Swap places so everyone has seen it from each position, and write down which motion was hardest to keep track of.

activities.title: A month of Moon sketches
activities.materials: A notebook, a pencil, and four weeks of clear evenings.
steps: Sketch the Moon's shape each evening and write the date beside it.
Mark every night you could not see it, and why - cloud, or it had not risen.
After four weeks, count the days from one full moon to the next.
Write down how close your figure came to 29 and a half days, and what would have made it more accurate.

activities.title: Pacing out the Solar System
activities.materials: A football, a few grains of sand, a long measuring tape or a known pace length, and a large open space.
steps: Put the football down as the Sun.
Pace out 25 metres and put a grain of sand there for the Earth.
Work out and pace out where Mars, Jupiter and Neptune would be, if you have room.
Write one sentence about what every textbook picture of the Solar System has to leave out.

rules.text: Moons orbit planets, planets orbit the Sun, and the Sun is a star.
Only a star makes its own light. Planets and moons shine by reflection.
The Moon is always half lit. The phases are how much of the lit half faces us.
Phases happen every month; eclipses are rare. They are not the same thing.

terms: Star
An object that makes its own light. The Sun is one.
Planet
A large object orbiting a star, shining only by reflected light.
Moon
A natural object orbiting a planet.
Satellite
Anything orbiting something larger - natural, like the Moon, or artificial.
Orbit
The curved path one object takes around another.
Axis
The imaginary line a planet spins around.
Solar System
The Sun and everything held in orbit by its gravity.
Asteroid
A rocky object, smaller than a planet, most of them between Mars and Jupiter.
Phase
The shape of the lit part of the Moon as seen from Earth.
New moon
The phase when the lit half faces away and we see almost nothing.
Full moon
The phase when the whole lit half faces us.
Waxing
When the lit part we can see is growing.
Waning
When the lit part we can see is shrinking.
commonMistakes: The Sun goes round the Earth.
The Earth spins, which makes the Sun appear to cross the sky. The Earth orbits the Sun, and not the other way round - it took careful records of the planets to settle it.
It is always a ball and always half lit. What changes is how much of the lit half we can see from where we are.
The phases are the Earth's shadow on the Moon.
That is an eclipse, and eclipses are rare. Phases happen every month, which alone shows they cannot be caused by an exact line-up.
The Moon has a permanently dark side.
The far side gets just as much sunlight. We never see it because the Moon turns once on its axis in exactly the time it takes to orbit us.
The Moon makes its own light.
Only stars do. The Moon reflects sunlight, which is why the lit part always faces the Sun.

connections.text: A month began as the Moon's cycle of phases, which is why it is about 29 or 30 days and not a round number.
Tides follow the Moon, so anyone launching a boat is using the Moon's position whether they name it or not.
A weather forecast and a map both arrive by artificial satellite - an object put into orbit to do deliberately what the Moon does naturally.
A month of sketches is a record, and a record settles an argument that memory cannot.

realProblems.context: Someone points at a very bright steady light in the evening sky and calls it the brightest star.
realProblems.prompt: How would you find out whether it is a star or a planet?
realProblems.answer: Look at whether it twinkles - stars do, planets shine steadily - and note its position against the star patterns, then check again a fortnight later. If it has moved against them it is a planet. It is very likely Venus.
realProblems.hint: One test works tonight; the better one needs two weeks.
realProblems.errorFeedback: A steady light that shifts against the star patterns over weeks is a planet, and Venus is the usual answer.

realProblems.context: A child says the Moon was broken last week because only a thin sliver of it was there.
realProblems.prompt: Explain what was really happening, in a way a younger child could follow.
realProblems.answer: The Moon is always a whole ball and the Sun always lights one half of it. Last week we were looking at it from an angle where almost all the lit half was turned away, so only a thin sliver showed. Nothing broke, and in two weeks the whole lit side will face us.
realProblems.hint: Use the ball and lamp - it is easier to show than to say.
realProblems.errorFeedback: The Moon is always a half-lit ball; the sliver was how much of the lit half faced us from here.

realProblems.context: A textbook diagram shows all eight planets neatly spaced across one page.
realProblems.prompt: What is the diagram right about and what is it badly wrong about, and why can it not do both?
realProblems.answer: It is right about the order and about everything orbiting the Sun. It is badly wrong about distance and size - on a true scale, if the Sun were a football the Earth would be a grain of sand 25 m away and Neptune 750 m off. It cannot do both, because a page that showed the distances truly would leave the planets invisibly small.
realProblems.hint: Ask what would have to shrink for the whole system to fit on a page.
realProblems.errorFeedback: The order is right, the distances are hugely compressed, and no single page can show both honestly.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain why the Moon appears to change shape during a month, when it never does.
keyIdeas: The Moon is always a half-lit ball
Our viewing angle changes as it orbits
The phases are how much of the lit half faces us
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: The Moon is a ball and the Sun always lights exactly half of it, just as it lights half the Earth. As the Moon travels round us our angle on that lit half changes, so we see different amounts of it - almost none at new moon, half of it a week later, all of it at full moon. The Moon itself does not change at all; only our view of it does.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: People once believed the Sun travels round the Earth. Explain why that was reasonable, and what settled it.
keyIdeas: It is exactly what the sky looks like
Records of the planets gave new evidence
The spin explains the same appearance
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: It is precisely what you see: the Sun rises on one side and sets on the other every day without fail, and with only your eyes that is the sensible conclusion. What settled it was careful records of where the planets appear night after night, whose looping paths only make sense if the Earth is one of the things going round the Sun. The Earth's own spin produces the same daily appearance, which is why the old idea fitted the evidence available at the time.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Some moons are larger than some planets. Explain how that can be true without the words losing their meaning.
keyIdeas: The difference is what it orbits, not how big it is
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: The words describe what an object goes round, not how large it is. A planet orbits a star; a moon orbits a planet. Jupiter's largest moons are bigger than Mercury, and they are still moons because they circle Jupiter rather than the Sun. If size decided it the categories would be useless, because there is no size that separates them.

questions.question: The Sun is:
questions.hint: It is the only thing in the Solar System making its own light.
questions.explanation: The Sun is an ordinary star. It looks special only because it is so much closer than all the others.

questions.question: Which planet is third from the Sun?
questions.explanation: The order outwards is Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, then the four giants.

questions.question: The Moon orbits:
questions.hint: A moon goes round a planet.
questions.explanation: The Moon orbits the Earth in about 27 days, while being carried round the Sun along with us.

questions.question: The Moon shines because it:
questions.hint: Only stars make their own light.
questions.explanation: The Moon has no light of its own, which is why the lit part always faces the Sun.

questions.question: Day and night are caused by:
options: the Earth spinning on its axis
the Sun going round the Earth
the Earth's orbit of the Sun
questions.answer: the Earth spinning on its axis
questions.explanation: The Earth turns once in 24 hours, so every place passes through the lit side and the dark side. The Sun does not move across the sky; we rotate past it.

questions.question: What holds the planets in orbit around the Sun?
questions.explanation: The Sun is so massive that its gravity reaches past Neptune, keeping each planet curving round instead of flying off in a straight line.

questions.question: The Moon's full cycle of phases takes about:
questions.hint: It is where the month came from.
questions.explanation: One full moon to the next is about 29 and a half days, which is why a month is roughly that length.

questions.question: At full moon, the Earth is:
options: roughly between the Sun and the Moon
questions.answer: roughly between the Sun and the Moon
questions.hint: We must be able to see the whole lit half.
questions.explanation: With the Earth between them, the Moon's sunlit half faces us and we see the complete circle.

questions.question: Why can the phases NOT be the Earth's shadow on the Moon?
options: phases happen every month, but exact line-ups are rare
the Moon is too far away
the Moon makes its own light
questions.answer: phases happen every month, but exact line-ups are rare
questions.hint: Compare how often phases happen with how often eclipses do.
questions.explanation: A shadow needs an exact line-up, which is an eclipse and happens a few times a year. Phases run their full cycle every month, so they must have another cause - our changing view.

questions.question: What makes something a moon rather than a planet?
options: it orbits a planet rather than a star
questions.answer: it orbits a planet rather than a star
questions.hint: Some moons are bigger than some planets.
questions.explanation: The words describe what an object goes round. Jupiter's largest moons beat Mercury for size and are still moons, because they circle Jupiter.
